name: Propositum
description: Watches the sources you approve, while a work session is running. Nothing else.
_comment_permissions: Every permission here is WARNING-FREE at install. Chrome shows no scary
prompt for any of them, which matters because a consumer product that asks
to 'read your browsing history' has already lost the argument it is trying
to make.
CORRECTED 2026-08-17 (ADR-0008; docs/research/intent-signals.md 2.1 and
4.1). Two of the three reasons below were wrong, and both are left in place
struck rather than deleted, because what they claimed is what a reader of
this file has believed since ADR-0002.
DELIBERATELY ABSENT — see ADR-0002:
tabs          would grant the URL and title of EVERY tab. WAS: 'without it
the extension is structurally incapable of learning the
person visited anything they did not approve; Chrome
enforces the constraint, not our code.' FALSE since
2026-08-11. chrome.tabs.query() needs no permission at all —
the permission only unscrubs url, pendingUrl, title and
favIconUrl on what comes back, and host_permissions
['https://*/*'] unscrubs them too. One line in
service-worker.js would return every open https tab today.
No line is that line. STILL ABSENT, and what holds it is
tests/extension-permissions.test.ts, which is our code
remembering — see docs/SECURITY_AND_PRIVACY.md, 'Data
explicitly not collected'.
webNavigation WAS: 'costs the Read your browsing history warning'. FALSE
since 2026-08-11. Under https://*/* Chrome's first host rule
absorbs kTab, kWebNavigation, kTopSites and kFavicon, so
adding this adds NO string to the install prompt and would
not even disable the extension pending re-approval. What is
still true is the part that was never the reason: it carries
transitionType — the most semantically loaded signal there
is ('typed it' vs 'followed a link'). We give it up and take
document.referrer plus Navigation Timing as partial
substitutes. The exclusion now stands on capability, and
ADR-0008 says what would have to be argued to take it.
history       not needed and not defensible. This one is unchanged: its
warning is NOT absorbed, and it is the one consumers know.
notifications is warning-free and is the ONLY way to surface an offer
nobody asked for. sidePanel.open() requires a user gesture, so calling it
from an alarm silently throws — which is exactly what happened: the app
named the subject correctly and the person saw nothing but a small dot.
_comment_debugger: REVERSAL. ADR-0002 listed `debugger` under 'explicitly NOT', with the
reason 'would make every constraint below advisory'. That was correct.
ADR-0010 grants it anyway, and the price is stated in that ADR's opening
paragraph rather than buried: it is the first decision in this series
whose net effect on safety is negative.
It is here because every job people actually want done — reply in this
thread, fill this form, pull my orders out of this account — lives behind
a session Propositum's own browser does not have and must not be given.
The alternative was copying a credential out of Chrome, which is worse in
every dimension: invisible to the person, revocable only by changing a
password, and it turns a bounded local mistake into a durable one.
What holds the line now that the permission is granted:
- The tab is one Propositum OPENED. chrome.debugger.getTargets is never
called, chrome.tabs.query and chrome.tabs.get are never called, and
chrome.tabs.create is the only source of a tab id in this extension.
CORRECTED 2026-08-17: this bullet used to end 'that constraint is still
enforced by Chrome refusing rather than by our code remembering, which
is the one place ADR-0002's original argument survives intact.' That
was false. tabs.query needs no permission, so nothing is being refused
— the four calls above are absent because nobody wrote them, and
tests/extension-permissions.test.ts is what keeps them absent. See the
tabs entry above and ADR-0010 section 1, both amended the same day.
- No Runtime domain, ever. Propositum never runs a line of its own
JavaScript inside a page the person is signed into. Clicks are
synthesised at coordinates; see extension/src/cdp.js.
- Chrome's own attachment bar is unsuppressible and its Cancel is a free
kill switch. src/overlay.js adds the layer Chrome's bar cannot: which
tab, in plain language, with a Stop.
- tests/extension-cdp.test.ts greps this extension for the calls that
must never appear. The extension has no build step, so the file under
review is the file Chrome runs and a grep is a real guard.
_comment_hosts: BROAD BY DECISION, and this reverses ADR-0002. Detection cannot work on
sources the person has not set up yet, and the whole point of the feature
is noticing work before they have told us about it. That costs Chrome's
'Read and change all your data on all websites' warning at install, which
is the honest price and is not hidden anywhere in the UI.
What limits the exposure is NOT the permission any more, so it has to be
the behaviour, and it is enforced in two places:
- content.js sends METADATA ONLY while no session is running: a cleaned
URL, a title, dwell and scroll. Never page text.
(2026-08-17: true of content.js and NOT of what the app receives on the
ambient path. flushAmbient in service-worker.js rebuilds the wire shape
field by field and omits scrollFraction, so no scroll leaves the
browser while no session is running. ADR-0008's capture row says why
that line has not simply been added.)
- the app holds those in memory, bounded and discarded, and they never
reach the ledger unless the person accepts an offer.
Full page text still begins only after a session starts on an approved
_comment_loopback: The app's own origin, and the ONLY entry here that is not warning-free.
A service worker fetch to http://127.0.0.1 is cross-origin, and the app
sends no CORS headers deliberately — CORS protects nothing on loopback,
which is why the transport has four controls of its own. Without this the
extension cannot reach the app at all: the health check fails, the badge
shows '!', and capture is silently OFF.
Pinned to the port in package.json's dev script; a test asserts they match.
_comment_key: Pinned so the extension id is stable. Without it the id changes if the repo
moves, and the Origin check on the loopback transport starts rejecting our
REPLACE before any real install — this is a placeholder.
